thread.title: Why Amazon's Stock Price Is Ripe For A Correction - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)

author: Robert Riesen
title: Why Amazon's Stock Price Is Ripe For A Correction - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)
text:
Yeah, I know, I'm mostly out on an island when it comes to my thoughts on Amazon ( AMZN ). Revenue growth has been impressive and I do believe the company is on its way to continue revolutionizing the e-commerce experience. With that being said, the valuation of the company stopped making sense to me a few years ago. I used to own the stock, but sold when it traded around $1,000/share. Sure, I wish I held onto it for the upside, but I still see the stock headed for a big correction. These are just a couple of the reasons why now is a good time to sell and a bad time to buy:
Amazon's revenue growth has been impressive, but this has not resulted in much economies of scale yet. Any historical revenue growth has basically been parred with equal operating expense growth, which is a concerning trend. Amazon's enterprise value puts it close to Apple ( AAPL ) and beyond other high-growth tech stocks like Facebook ( FB ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ). The main issue is that Amazon is a long way from achieving what those companies have in terms of free cash flow (the most important performance metric in my opinion). I simply don't buy stocks based on performance expectations that might be a decade away. Much of Amazon's stock price increase can be explained by an increasing Price/Sales multiple. This is often a red flag for me. I like to see price increases that are mostly explained by improving performance and less so on valuation multiples being stretched. Amazon's Impressive First Quarter, Sort Of Below is a snapshot from Amazon's Q1 earnings release . The 42.9% increase in sales year over year is impressive. That is until you dig into some of the other numbers. The problem I see is that operating expense also increased 41.5%. Amazon is still having a hard time reaching economies of scale, even with $51 billion in sales for the quarter.
Amazon bulls contest that Amazon is just investing in its growth and one day costs will be trimmed and the profit machine will be turned on, but I don't really see it that way. I stated this in a previous article , and it's worth stating again. Most of what Amazon recognizes in operating expense (per GAAP) is what was spent to produce that revenue. Investments into software, data centers, and fulfillment centers get logged into fixed assets and get depreciated over a long period of time. A much more logical assessment is that Amazon's costs to run its business are increasing and economies of scale haven't yet materialized. No company spends money they don't have to, so I assume that Amazon needs to keep spending substantial amounts of money to sustain its growth.
When I look at the expense lines, I also don't really see that much that can be cut. Cost of sales and fulfillment will continue to rise as revenue increases. Gross margins have been improving, but rising fulfillment costs have been an issue for the company. Amazon doesn't spend much on marketing or administratively. Technology and content expense is the main line item I could see savings in the future. Altogether, Amazon was only able to turn its monster $51 billion in revenue into a measly $1.9 billion in operating income, which leaves me rather unimpressed.
Amazon's Free Cash Flow Production I look to free cash flow more than any other performance or valuation metric. While Amazon's numbers below aren't bad, they just don't match up to its enterprise value, which currently stands at $852 billion.
Data Source: Amazon's SEC Filings The problem is, Amazon is so far behind some of its technology peers. Since Amazon is valued almost as much as Apple, there's theoretical expectations that one day the company will get to more than $50 billion in free cash flow. But here's my point, when will Amazon achieve those figures, if ever? I believe the company can get to that level of performance, but it could be 10 years from now, or more. Would you buy a stock that's valued on performance levels that far in advance? I sure wouldn't, there's just too much uncertainty and risk for that.
This disparity is also evident when looking at EV/FCF. Even if I used Amazon's best year of free cash flow production (i.e., 2016 at $10.5 billion), its EV/FCF multiple would still be 80.9x. I'll take Facebook's EV/FCF of 26.86x and a similar growth rate any day of the week.
Free Cash Flow corresponds to the trailing 12 months for each company Growth rates provided by Reuters Amazon's Runaway Price/Sales Multiple Margin improvements and improving free cash flow are a few things that can rationally explain Price/Sales multiple increases. Looking at Amazon's performance over time, you'll see that there's been improvement in gross margins, but that hasn't translated into great operating or profit margins.
Out of all valuation multiples, Amazon's increasing Price/Sales multiple is the one I struggle with the most. From 2014 to 2016, the range was generally between 1.6x and 2.4x. At the time, that was considered a very rich multiple. Now the multiple is approximately twice that and I have a tough time rationally understanding this. Modest operating and profit margin improvements haven't been enough for this valuation boost in my opinion. This has been one of the driving forces in Amazon's stock price increase over the last couple of years (see chart below).
For comparison, Walmart's ( WMT ) Price/Sales Multiple is 0.49x and Apple's is 3.75x. In terms of operating profit, Walmart's was $20.4 billion and Apple's was $61.3 billion in the last fiscal year.
AMZN data by YCharts
Conclusion Amazon's stock price continues to increase unchecked. While the company has made some impressive achievements, there's still plenty of weakness evident. The stock price trajectory will soon put Amazon's valuation ahead of Apple's. In my opinion, Apple is the greatest company of all-time and has reached performance levels that have been unmatched and Amazon isn't even close. Amazon might some day reach those levels, but that's a long way off. When expectations are that high, so is the risk and the risk vs. reward profile of Amazon doesn't look good. Now looks like a great time to sell, recognize profits, and find value elsewhere. I will continue to point out that much of Amazon's stock price run-up over the last couple of years has been a result of an increasing Price/Sales multiple and irrational performance expectations. Amazon has yet to demonstrate it can turn its increasing sales into meaningful operating margin, profits, and free cash flow.
Disclosure: I am/we are long FB, AAPL.
